case_study_insert.main_stem: Norhaven Technical Fasteners (NTF) is a public limited company in the metal components sector, producing threaded fasteners for construction equipment and exporting to three continents, with a workforce of 85. Founded in 1998 by Soren Norhaven, it uses a flat organisational structure and laissez-faire leadership. NTF will invest $1,080,000 in an automated thread-rolling line, financed by a $600,000 share issue, a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $26.00, and produces 60,000 units a year. NTF suffers labour turnover of 14% and a 3.4% defect rate on threaded components, delaying shipments to distributors.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q2 2025: 15,200 fasteners were sampled; the defect rate was 3.4%, down from 5.1%. There were 47 customer complaints about thread stripping, against 61 a year before. Average delivery lead time is 18 days and 91% of orders arrive on time. Rework cost $7,200 last quarter. A survey of 350 purchasing managers found 63% value certified thread quality and 49% would switch supplier for a 2% price cut.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Norhaven Technical Fasteners as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate rose from 4.50% to 5.25%, raising the cost of bank borrowing. (2) The minimum wage increased 4.9% to $13.80 per hour. (3) Alloy steel and nickel input costs rose 11.2% year-on-year, while engineering wage inflation reached 5.6% and export demand grew 2.4%.

questions.question_text: NTF plans to finance part of its thread-rolling line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for NTF of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $600,000 share issue brings equity that needs no interest and no fixed repayment dates, leaving the $300,000 bank loan as the only debt commitment. With fixed costs of $420,000 a year and output of 60,000 units, that protects cash flow and lets Soren Norhaven direct funds to reducing the 3.4% defect rate rather than servicing debt.

Point 2: Equity widens NTF's shareholder base and spreads the risk of the $1,080,000 investment across investors instead of pledging company assets. As a public limited company it can access many shareholders, so the automated line can be funded without pushing the 85-worker business further into borrowing, though existing shareholders would be diluted.

For a public limited company with 85 workers and $420,000 fixed costs, equity also avoids the risk that a 5.25% base rate raises the $300,000 loan cost further. Shareholders share the risk of the $1,080,000 line in return for dividends, whereas a lender must be paid whether or not the 3.4% defect rate is fixed, so the $600,000 issue protects the 25,000-unit margin of safety.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: NTF is launching a certified thread-quality range. Consider trade-journal advertising, an industry exhibition, or technical webinars for purchasing managers. Which should NTF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade-journal advertising: Specialist engineering journals reach the 63% of surveyed managers who value certified thread quality at low cost per reader, but static pages cannot prove the 3.4% defect rate improvement and the message is easily ignored.

Industry exhibition: An exhibition allows live demonstration of the thread-rolling line and face-to-face discussion of the 18-day lead time and 91% on-time record. It suits a component sold on trust. Yet stand costs are high and with 14% labour turnover the staff showing the product may lack product knowledge, and only a small number of buyers attend.

Technical webinars: Live online sessions can show tolerance data to purchasing managers across three continents, record the session for later viewing and directly address the 49% who would switch for a 2% price cut. They are cheap and scalable, though engagement depends on promotion and cannot reproduce hands-on inspection.

Reach must be weighed against the 25,000-unit margin of safety: with $12.00 contribution, roughly 2,083 extra units recover a $25,000 campaign, and that can be checked against the 350 surveyed managers. Webinars collect qualified leads across three continents and address the 49% who would switch for a 2% price cut, whereas a broad exhibition audience would not justify the $1,080,000 commitment.

Certification evidence from the 15,200 sampled fasteners should be shown in each session, since 63% of managers value it.

Recommendation: NTF should choose technical webinars, backed by short journal adverts. They reach the exact surveyed audience cheaply and demonstrate certification across export markets. Exhibitions are rejected as costly and exposed by labour turnover; journals alone are rejected because they cannot demonstrate quality.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two promotional options applied to NTF with emerging judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options in context with a justified recommendation that rejects exhibitions and journals.

questions.question_text: NTF has labour turnover of 14% and uses laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for NTF of introducing regular appraisal and team working for its workforce of 85.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Regular appraisal gives each of the 85 workers feedback and agreed targets, replacing the drift that laissez-faire leadership can allow on the thread-rolling line. Clear expectations and recognition address the causes of 14% labour turnover, keeping skilled operators who are needed to sustain the fall in defect rate from 5.1% to 3.4% and protect the $1,080,000 investment.

Point 2: Team working lets experienced setters share knowledge about thread stripping, directly reducing the 47 complaints and the $7,200 rework cost. Under Maslow's social and esteem needs, belonging to a team raises commitment, so delivery lead time of 18 days and the 91% on-time rate are more likely to hold while production reaches 60,000 units.

Productivity is 60,000 units divided by 85 workers, or 705.88 units per worker, so retaining skilled setters protects that ratio and the $12.00 contribution. Appraisal and team working also support the 91% on-time figure and 18-day lead time that matter to the 63% of surveyed managers who value certified thread quality.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: NTF needs skilled operators for its new line. Consider internal promotion or external recruitment to reduce its 14% labour turnover. Which should NTF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal promotion: Promoting existing workers rewards loyalty, cuts the 14% turnover and needs no advertising or induction costs. Promoted staff already know NTF's processes, so the 3.4% defect rate and 18-day lead time are less likely to rise. The limitation is that the workforce of 85 may not contain enough thread-rolling skills, so promotion can simply move a skills gap elsewhere.

External recruitment: Hiring experienced setters brings new techniques and immediately fills the skill gap for the $1,080,000 line, helping cut the 47 complaints. It costs advertising and selection time, needs induction, and can demoralise existing staff, raising turnover further if outsiders are preferred.

The plan should be measured against the 3.4% defect rate, the 47 complaints and the $7,200 rework bill, keeping 91% of orders on time during the change. External hires would need induction on the $1,080,000 line, which could disrupt the 18-day lead time just as NTF seeks certified contracts. The insert gives no promotion costs or course fees, so none are invented; the decision rests on the 14% turnover problem and the 35,000-unit break-even across 85 staff.

Keeping the 85-strong team intact also protects the $21.00 unit-cost benchmark and the 18-day lead time while the new line beds in.

Decision: NTF should choose internal promotion first, with targeted external recruitment only for skills absent from the 85-strong team. Promotion tackles the 14% turnover directly and protects morale and the $7,200 rework saving; wholesale external hiring is rejected because it would cost more and could worsen the turnover problem it is meant to solve.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of internal and external recruitment applied to NTF's turnover and skills needs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both recruitment routes with a justified decision rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NTF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($26.00 − $14.00) = $420,000 ÷ $12.00 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $26.00 − $14.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NTF's management can use this cost, break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the break-even output of 35,000 units with actual production of 60,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 25,000 units, so they know how far demand can fall before NTF makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 shows what each unit adds towards fixed costs of $420,000; for illustration, a $1.00 price cut would reduce contribution to $11.00 and raise break-even to 38,181.82 units, letting managers test pricing before committing.
3. Average total cost of $21.00 a unit ($420,000 ÷ 60,000 units plus $14.00 variable cost) provides a benchmark each quarter to track the 14% labour turnover and 3.4% defect rate and decide whether rework is pushing unit cost above plan.
4. Labour productivity of 705.88 units per worker (60,000 units ÷ workforce of 85) shows whether the $1,080,000 investment can be handled by the existing team, or whether recruitment is needed before the wage bill rises.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 60,000 units; illustrative pricing and the $420,000 fixed costs; the $1,080,000 investment decision; and unit-cost and productivity benchmarking to tackle the 14% labour turnover and 3.4% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NTF's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has NTF's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios is the stronger evidence? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.72 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 2.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.15 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $165,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $430,000; 2025 current assets = $195,000 + $185,000 + $80,000 = $460,000. For 2024, $430,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.72, and ($430,000 − $210,000) ÷ $250,000 = 0.88. For 2025, $460,000 ÷ $230,000 = 2.00, and ($460,000 − $195,000) ÷ $230,000 = 1.15. All source figures are the $'000 values in Appendix 2.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures, so NTF's short-term financial position has improved. Current assets grew from $430,000 to $460,000 while current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $230,000, and cash rose from $55,000 to $80,000, giving a stronger cushion for the $300,000 bank loan; however receivables rose from $165,000 to $185,000, tying up cash.
The acid test ratio is the stronger evidence of real improvement because it rose from 0.88 to 1.15 without relying on inventories, which are the least liquid current asset.

These are single-year snapshots with no sector benchmark in the insert, and a 2.00 current ratio could indicate idle cash rather than efficiency. The $185,000 receivables and $195,000 inventories should be checked for collectability and obsolescence before the $1,080,000 line is committed.

Conclusion: NTF's financial position has improved: both liquidity measures are higher in 2025 and the gain survives the exclusion of inventories. NTF should keep control of the larger receivables balance while the $1,080,000 line is commissioned.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with some contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities, an explicit answer on the stronger ratio, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NTF of using automated thread rolling instead of manual threading.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automation can reproduce precise threads consistently, reducing the 3.4% defect rate and the $7,200 rework cost, so more of the 60,000 units meet the 63% of buyers who value certification and the $12.00 contribution is protected despite fixed costs of $420,000.

Disadvantage: The automated line raises fixed costs and requires the 85 workers to learn new skills while labour turnover is 14%, so initial disruption could delay the 18-day lead time. The $14.00 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, and with alloy steel up 11.2% an automated process may be less able to switch suppliers than manual methods.

The $1,080,000 line raises fixed costs from the present $420,000, so NTF must still sell 35,000 units to break even while 11.2% alloy costs press on the $14.00 variable cost. The insert gives no output gain from automation, so none is claimed; the case rests on reducing the 3.4% defect rate and the $7,200 rework bill to protect the 25,000-unit margin of safety.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase to $13.80 and the 11.2% rise in alloy steel and nickel input costs will affect NTF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
NTF faces three external changes reported in Appendix 3.

Base interest rate 4.50% to 5.25%: If the $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 bank loan = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × 300,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $420,000 and the $1,080,000 investment, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it completely, though future borrowing would cost more and customers may cut spending.

Minimum wage up 4.9% to $13.80: With a workforce of 85, this raises the wage bill on every production hour and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay rates, so no defensible annual total can be invented; against the given productivity of 705.88 units per worker, the rise is absorbable only if output per worker holds, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

11.2% alloy steel and nickel input costs: The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost per unit, so only a labelled upper-bound illustration is honest: if the entire $14.00 were exposed, the rise would add 0.112 × $14.00 = $1.568 a unit, or $94,080 a year at 60,000 units. This bound is well above the $2,250 interest effect and shows why supplier negotiation matters more than loan terms.

Conclusion: the 11.2% rise in alloy steel and nickel input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 60,000 units, directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $1,080,000 plan, and dwarfs the $2,250 interest effect; the wage rise is material but cannot be quantified from the insert. Soren Norhaven should lock in alloy prices and use the certified-quality reputation rather than chase cheaper borrowing.
